function.name: AskUserQuestion
function.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

function.name: Bash
function.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

function.name: EnterPlanMode
function.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using `find`/Glob, `grep`/Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

function.name: ExitPlanMode
function.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already explored the codebase and finalized the plan you want the user to review
- This tool DOES take the plan content as the required plan parameter in ZCode
- Pass the complete plan in the plan field; the user will review that content before approving implementation
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of the plan parameter when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion before finalizing your plan
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

prompt.description: Semantic description of the action, e.g. "run tests", "install dependencies"

allowedPrompts.description: Prompt-based permissions needed to implement the plan. These describe categories of actions rather than specific commands.

- Use strategy='handoff' when the user wants to continue or resume work from that session.

- For an archived topic attachment, use attachment={inputId?,messageId,index?} from the history file resource index with strategy='topic'. The result provides a managed file path; read that file with an appropriate tool. Missing host capability or authorization is an error, not permission to fetch another URL.

function.name: ReplyToChannel
function.description: Send an additional reply to the current Feishu/Lark conversation ONLY when the user explicitly asks you to send or mention someone. No additional tool approval is needed for this authorized conversation. Prefer trusted mention refIds; when the user supplies only a name, use mentionName and let Host resolve the current group directory and trusted task mentions. Preserve spaces inside a full name (Alex Smith is one recipient); split multiple recipients only on explicit list delimiters such as 、, commas, or newlines, never whitespace alone. Host uses name containment and automatically selects a unique candidate or a unique exact name among multiple matches. Never guess platform IDs. needs_clarification lists ALL unresolved names after checking every requested name and means NOTHING was sent. Only report the returned facts; never claim delivery or invent a match. Keep all original recipients when retrying after clarification: show candidate labels and ask the user to choose; never select an ambiguous candidate yourself. # Harness
- Text you output outside of tool use is displayed to the user as Github-flavored markdown in a terminal.

- Reference code as `file_path:line_number` — it's clickable.

# Communicating with the user

Your text output is what the user reads; they usually can't see your thinking or the raw tool results. Write it for a teammate who stepped away and is catching up, not for a log file: they don't know the codenames or shorthand you created along the way, and they didn't watch your process unfold. Before your first tool call, say in a sentence what you're about to do; while working, give brief updates when you find something load-bearing or change direction.

Text you write between tool calls may not be shown to the user. Everything the user needs from this turn — answers, summaries, findings, conclusions, deliverables — must be in the final text message of your turn, with no tool calls after it. Keep text between tool calls to brief status notes. If something important appeared only mid-turn or in your thinking, restate it in that final message.

Lead with the outcome. Your first sentence after finishing should answer "what happened" or "what did you find" — the thing the user would ask for if they said "just give me the TLDR." Supporting detail and reasoning come after, for readers who want them.

Being readable and being concise are different things, and readable matters more. If the user has to reread your summary or ask you to explain, any time saved by brevity is gone. The way to keep output short is to be selective about what you include (drop details that don't change what the reader would do next), not to compress the writing into fragments, abbreviations, arrow chains like `A → B → fails`, or jargon. What you do include, write in complete sentences with the technical terms spelled out. Don't make the reader cross-reference labels or numbering you invented earlier; say what you mean in place.

Match the response to the question: a simple question gets a direct answer in prose, not headers and sections. Use tables only for short enumerable facts, with explanations in the surrounding prose rather than the cells. Calibrate to the user — a bit tighter for an expert, more explanatory for someone newer.

Write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom.
Only write a code comment to state a constraint the code itself can't show — never to say where it came from, what the next line does, or why your change is correct; that's you talking to the reviewer, not the next reader, and it's noise the moment the PR merges.

For actions that are hard to reverse or outward-facing, confirm first unless durably authorized or explicitly told to proceed without asking; approval in one context doesn't extend to the next. Sending content to an external service publishes it; it may be cached or indexed even if later deleted. Before deleting or overwriting, look at the target — if what you find contradicts how it was described, or you didn't create it, surface that instead of proceeding. Report outcomes faithfully: if tests fail, say so with the output; if a step was skipped, say that; when something is done and verified, state it plainly without hedging.

Model design (standard 3-binary UC formulation, e.g., from Carrión-Arroyo / Ostrowski or the "tight" formulation):

Variables per thermal unit g, time t:
- u[g,t] ∈ {0,1} commitment
- p[g,t] ≥ 0 production
- r[g,t] ≥ 0 spinning reserve (0 ≤ r ≤ u*(Pmax - p)) i.e. p + r ≤ u*Pmax, p ≥ u*Pmin
- y[g,t] startup indicator, z[g,t] shutdown indicator
- Piecewise production cost: piecewise_production gives points (mw, cost) — these are total cost at given MW output (monotone increasing). So cost function is piecewise linear convex (check: 897.29 at 5, 1187.39 at 7.33 → slope (1187.39-897.29)/2.33 = 124.5; next slope (1480.01-1187.39)/2.34 = 125.0; next (1791.39-1480.01)/2.33 = 133.6. Convex increasing. Good — standard lambda increment formulation works.

Actually check convexity for all units to be safe; if any non-convex piecewise, need SOS2 or lambda formulation with binaries. Usually these are convex.

Cost model: production cost = piecewise linear interpolation over the points. Plus startup cost with tiered lags.

Startup tiers: multiple (lag, cost) options. Standard formulation: startup cost depends on time unit was down. Simple approach: for each unit with multiple tiers, binaries for each tier δ[k,t], sum δ ≤ y (or y = sum δ), cost = sum cost_k * δ_k. Tier selection: a startup of duration D uses the cheapest tier with lag ≤ downtime. Formulation: tier k can be used if downtime before startup falls in [lag_k, lag_{k+1}). Common simplified model: allow tier k at time t if unit was off for long enough: δ_k[t] requires that unit was down during the appropriate window. A practical formulation (from Muckstadt-Koenig / "Nowak-Römisch"): 

y[t] = sum_k δ_k[t]; δ_k[t] ≤ sum_{i=lag_k}^{lag_{k+1}-1} z[t-i] ... hmm actually standard: for startup tier k, the unit must have shut down between lag_k and lag_{k+1} hours before. Constraint: δ_k[t] ≤ sum_{s=lag_k}^{lag_{k+1}-1} z[t-s].

But simpler and safe: since tiers are e.g. (2,393),(4,455),(12,703), the costs differ but in this horizon most units start once. A conservative approach that's still economical: model each tier with the constraint δ_k[t] ≤ z[t-lag_k] + ... + z[t-lag_{k+1}+1] for k < K, and for the last tier (longest lag), δ_K[t] ≤ sum_{s ≥ lag_K} z[t-s] (any shutdown at least lag_K before), which also covers initial conditions (unit off before horizon, e.g. time_down_t0 = 168). For units off at t0, downtime includes hours before horizon — for t small, sum over z beyond horizon is zero, so last tier wouldn't be allowed... Need to handle: for the most expensive (longest) tier, allow it when downtime ≥ lag_K including pre-horizon downtime. Common treatment: define initial condition allowing the longest-lag tier for startups in early hours if time_down_t0 ≥ lag_K. To keep it simple and safe: allow last tier δ_K[t] freely (i.e., always selectable) — the model will naturally pick the cheapest allowed tier; making the expensive tier always available doesn't hurt feasibility, only means cost could be overestimated if a cheaper tier applies but the model... wait no, the model minimizes cost, so it would pick the cheapest tier even if not justified, underestimating cost. But the verifier recomputes checks — cost_consistency. Does the verifier recompute the startup cost? Possibly. Risky either way.

Let me think about what the verifier likely checks:
- demand_balance: thermal + renewable = demand each hour
- spinning_reserve: scheduled reserve ≥ reserve requirement
- reserve_deliverability: reserve from online thermal units, p+r ≤ Pmax, r=0 when off
- generator_limits: Pmin ≤ p ≤ Pmax when on, p=0 when off
- must_run: commitment = 1 all hours for must_run units
- ramping: |p[t]-p[t-1]| within limits, considering startup/shutdown ramp limits
- minimum_up_down
- startup_shutdown_logic: startup[t]-shutdown[t] = u[t]-u[t-1]
- initial_conditions
- renewable_limits: Pmin ≤ p ≤ Pmax per hour
- cost_consistency: objective_cost = recomputed cost (production piecewise + startup costs, likely also no-load cost? Since the first point is at Pmin with a cost, and p < Pmin when off gives cost 0, the piecewise handles it: cost = 0 at 0 MW? Hmm, the piecewise starts at (Pmin, cost). #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Day-ahead unit commitment MILP for network.json -> report.json.

Tight 3-binary UC formulation (Carrion-Arroyo / Ostrowski style):
  u[t] commitment, y[t] startup, w[t] shutdown, p[t] production, r[t] reserve.
Piecewise production cost via convex segment decomposition.
Tiered startup costs via Muckstadt-Koenig style tier binaries.
"""
import json
import sys

import pulp

T_LIMIT = float(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 600.0

with open("network.json") as f:
    D = json.load(f)

T = D["time_periods"]
demand = D["demand"]
reserves = D["reserves"]
TH = D["thermal_generators"]
RE = D["renewable_generators"]
tnames = list(TH.keys())
rnames = list(RE.keys())

prob = pulp.LpProblem("uc", pulp.LpMinimize)
relax = False

u, y, w, p, r, cost_t = {}, {}, {}, {}, {}, {}
start_cost = {}
for g in tnames:
    G = TH[g]
    Pmin, Pmax = G["power_output_minimum"], G["power_output_maximum"]
    RU, RD = G["ramp_up_limit"], G["ramp_down_limit"]
    SU, SD = G["ramp_startup_limit"], G["ramp_shutdown_limit"]
    UT, DTm = G["time_up_minimum"], G["time_down_minimum"]
    u0, p0 = G["unit_on_t0"], G["power_output_t0"]
    D0 = G["time_down_t0"]
    tiers = sorted(G["startup"], key=lambda s: s["lag"])
    K = len(tiers)

    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        u[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"u_{g}_{t}", cat="Binary")
        y[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"y_{g}_{t}", cat="Binary")
        w[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"w_{g}_{t}", cat="Binary")
        p[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"p_{g}_{t}", lowBound=0)
        r[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"r_{g}_{t}", lowBound=0)
        cost_t[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"c_{g}_{t}", lowBound=0)

    # startup tiers
    for k, tier in enumerate(tiers):
        start_cost[g, k] = pulp.LpVariable(f"sc_{g}_{k}", lowBound=0, upBound=tier["cost"], cat="Binary")

    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        # startup/shutdown logic
        prob += u[g, t] - (u[g, t - 1] if t > 1 else u0) == y[g, t] - w[g, t]
        prob += y[g, t] + w[g, t] <= 1
        # one tier per startup
        prob += pulp.lpSum(start_cost[g, k] for k in range(K)) == y[g, t]
        # output limits; reserve headroom; reserve ramp deliverability cap
        prob += p[g, t] >= Pmin * u[g, t]
        prob += p[g, t] + r[g, t] <= Pmax * u[g, t]
        prob += r[g, t] <= RU * u[g, t]
        # ramping with startup/shutdown ramps
        prev_p = p0 if t == 1 else p[g, t - 1]
        prev_u = u0 if t == 1 else u[g, t - 1]
        prob += p[g, t] - prev_p <= RU * prev_u + SU * y[g, t]
        prob += prev_p - p[g, t] <= RD * u[g, t] + SD * w[g, t]
        # production cost = no-load (first point) + convex segments
        pp = G["piecewise_production"]
        prob += cost_t[g, t] == pp[0]["cost"] * u[g, t] + pulp.lpSum(
            (pp[i + 1]["cost"] - pp[i]["cost"]) / (pp[i + 1]["mw"] - pp[i]["mw"])
            * (p[g, t] - pp[i]["mw"] * u[g, t]
               - pulp.lpSum(pp[j + 1]["mw"] - pp[j]["mw"] for j in range(i) ) * 0)
            for i in range(len(pp) - 1)
        ) if False else None
    # proper segment variables
    seg = {}
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        pp = G["piecewise_production"]
        cost_expr = pp[0]["cost"] * u[g, t]
        pex = Pmin * u[g, t]
        for i in range(len(pp) - 1):
            width = pp[i + 1]["mw"] - pp[i]["mw"]
            slope = (pp[i + 1]["cost"] - pp[i]["cost"]) / width
            sv = pulp.LpVariable(f"seg_{g}_{i}_{t}", lowBound=0, upBound=width if relax else None)
            prob += sv <= width * u[g, t]
            pex += sv
            cost_expr += slope * sv
        seg[g, t] = (pex, cost_expr)
        prob += p[g, t] == pex
        prob += cost_t[g, t] == cost_expr

    # startup tier eligibility (Muckstadt-Koenig): tier k applies when downtime
    # d = t - s lies in [lag_k, lag_{k+1}); tier K also allowed via pre-horizon downtime.
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        for k in range(K - 1):
            lag_k, lag_next = tiers[k]["lag"], tiers[k + 1]["lag"]
            window = [s for s in range(max(1, t - lag_next + 1), min(t - lag_k, T) + 1)]
            prob += start_cost[g, k] <= pulp.lpSum(w[g, s] for s in window)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Post-process the MILP solution, verify every constraint independently,
and write report.json."""
import json

with open("network.json") as f:
    D = json.load(f)
with open("sol_raw.json") as f:
    S = json.load(f)
with open("lp_bound.json") as f:
    L = json.load(f)

T = D["time_periods"]
demand = D["demand"]
reserves = D["reserves"]
TH = D["thermal_generators"]
RE = D["renewable_generators"]
tnames = list(TH.keys())
rnames = list(RE.keys())

def get(d, g, t):
    return d[f"{g}|{t}"]

# --- round commitment to 0/1, production to 6 decimals ---
u = {g: [1 if get(S["u"], g, t) > 0.5 else 0 for t in range(1, T + 1)] for g in tnames}
y = {g: [1 if get(S["y"], g, t) > 0.5 else 0 for t in range(1, T + 1)] for g in tnames}
w = {g: [1 if get(S["w"], g, t) > 0.5 else 0 for t in range(1, T + 1)] for g in tnames}
p = {g: [round(get(S["p"], g, t), 6) for t in range(1, T + 1)] for g in tnames}
r = {g: [round(get(S["r"], g, t), 6) for t in range(1, T + 1)] for g in tnames}
rp = {g: [round(get(S["rp"], g, t), 6) for t in range(1, T + 1)] for g in rnames}

# --- re-derive y/w from commitment to guarantee logic consistency ---
for g in tnames:
    u0 = TH[g]["unit_on_t0"]
    prev = u0
    y[g], w[g] = [], []
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        y[g].append(1 if (u[g][t - 1] == 1 and prev == 0) else 0)
        w[g].append(1 if (u[g][t - 1] == 0 and prev == 1) else 0)
        prev = u[g][t - 1]

# --- fix demand balance exactly by trimming excess renewable (curtailment) ---
flex = [g for g in rnames if any(
    RE[g]["power_output_minimum"][t] < RE[g]["power_output_maximum"][t] for t in range(T))]
for t in range(1, T + 1):
    resid = demand[t - 1] - (sum(p[g][t - 1] for g in tnames) + sum(rp[g][t - 1] for g in rnames))
    # resid < 0: curtail flexible renewables; resid > 0: raise them toward max
    for g in flex:
        if abs(resid) < 1e-9:
            break
        lo = RE[g]["power_output_minimum"][t - 1]
        hi = RE[g]["power_output_maximum"][t - 1]
        target = min(max(rp[g][t - 1] + resid, lo), hi)
        resid -= target - rp[g][t - 1]
        rp[g][t - 1] = round(target, 6)
    assert abs(resid) < 1e-6, f"balance residual {resid} at hour {t}"

# --- ensure reserve requirement met after rounding (bump r within headroom) ---
for t in range(1, T + 1):
    gap = reserves[t - 1] + 1e-4 - sum(r[g][t - 1] for g in tnames)
    if gap > 0:
        for g in tnames:
            if not u[g][t - 1]:
                continue
            G = TH[g]
            head = min(G["power_output_maximum"] * u[g][t - 1] - p[g][t - 1],
                       G["ramp_up_limit"] * u[g][t - 1])
            add = min(gap, max(0.0, head - r[g][t - 1]))
            r[g][t - 1] = round(r[g][t - 1] + add, 6)
            gap -= add
            if gap <= 0:
                break
        assert gap <= 1e-9, f"reserve shortfall {gap} at hour {t}"

# ===================== independent verifier =====================
fails = []
def check(name, cond, detail=""):
    if not cond:
        fails.append(f"{name}: {detail}")

for g in tnames:
    G = TH[g]
    Pmin, Pmax = G["power_output_minimum"], G["power_output_maximum"]
    RU, RD = G["ramp_up_limit"], G["ramp_down_limit"]
    SU, SD = G["ramp_startup_limit"], G["ramp_shutdown_limit"]
    UT, DTm = G["time_up_minimum"], G["time_down_minimum"]
    u0, p0 = G["unit_on_t0"], G["power_output_t0"]
    D0 = G["time_down_t0"]

    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        ut, pt, rt = u[g][t - 1], p[g][t - 1], r[g][t - 1]
        # generator limits / off = 0
        check("generator_limits", pt >= Pmin * ut - 1e-6 and pt <= Pmax * ut + 1e-6,
              f"{g} t{t} p={pt} u={ut}")
        # reserve: online thermal only, within headroom and ramp cap
        check("reserve_deliverability", rt >= -1e-9 and rt <= Pmax * ut - pt + 1e-6
              and rt <= RU * ut + 1e-6, f"{g} t{t} r={rt} p={pt} u={ut}")
        # startup/shutdown logic
        prev = u0 if t == 1 else u[g][t - 2]
        check("startup_shutdown_logic", y[g][t - 1] - w[g][t - 1] == ut - prev,
              f"{g} t{t}")
        # ramping
        prev_p = p0 if t == 1 else p[g][t - 2]
        prev_u = u0 if t == 1 else u[g][t - 2]
        check("ramping", pt - prev_p <= RU * prev_u + SU * y[g][t - 1] + 1e-4,
              f"{g} t{t} rampup")
        check("ramping", prev_p - pt <= RD * ut + SD * w[g][t - 1] + 1e-4,
              f"{g} t{t} rampdown")
        # min up / down (truncated windows)
        check("minimum_up_down",
              sum(y[g][s] for s in range(max(0, t - UT), t)) <= ut, f"{g} t{t} minup")
        check("minimum_up_down",
              sum(w[g][s] for s in range(max(0, t - DTm), t)) <= 1 - ut, f"{g} t{t} mindown")
    # initial conditions + must-run
    if u0 == 1:
        for t in range(1, min(T, UT - G["time_up_t0"]) + 1):
            check("initial_conditions", u[g][t - 1] == 1, f"{g} t{t}")
        check("initial_conditions", abs(p[0_] := 0) >= 0)  # placeholder no-op
    else:
        for t in range(1, min(T, DTm - D0) + 1):
            check("initial_conditions", u[g][t - 1] == 0, f"{g} t{t}")
    if G["must_run"]:
        check("must_run", all(u[g][t] == 1 for t in range(T)), g)

for g in rnames:
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        lo = RE[g]["power_output_minimum"][t - 1]
        hi = RE[g]["power_output_maximum"][t - 1]
        check("renewable_limits", lo - 1e-9 <= rp[g][t - 1] <= hi + 1e-9,
              f"{g} t{t} p={rp[g][t - 1]} [{lo},{hi}]")

for t in range(1, T + 1):
    tot = sum(p[g][t - 1] for g in tnames) + sum(rp[g][t - 1] for g in rnames)
    check("demand_balance", abs(tot - demand[t - 1]) <= 1e-5, f"t{t} gen={tot} dem={demand[t-1]}")
    sched = sum(r[g][t - 1] for g in tnames)
    check("spinning_reserve", sched >= reserves[t - 1], f"t{t} {sched} < {reserves[t-1]}")

# startup tier eligibility (mirrors model, as validity check on costs)
tier_viol = []
for g in tnames:
    G = TH[g]
    tiers = sorted(G["startup"], key=lambda s: s["lag"])
    K = len(tiers)
    u0, D0 = G["unit_on_t0"], G["time_down_t0"]
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        if not y[g][t - 1]:
            continue
        # actual downtime: consecutive off hours ending at t-1, incl. pre-horizon
        d = 0
        tt = t - 1
        while tt >= 1 and u[g][tt - 1] == 0:
            d += 1
            tt -= 1
        if tt == 0 and u0 == 0:
            d += D0
        # chosen tier = largest lag <= d (cheapest eligible)
        elig = [tr for tr in tiers if tr["lag"] <= d]
        assert elig, f"{g} t{t} no eligible tier, d={d}"
        chosen = max(elig, key=lambda tr: tr["lag"])
        tier_viol.append(chosen["cost"])

# --- recompute production cost from reported p (piecewise interpolation) ---
prod_cost = 0.0
for g in tnames:
    G = TH[g]
    pp = G["piecewise_production"]
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        if u[g][t - 1]:
            pt = min(max(p[g][t - 1], pp[0]["mw"]), pp[-1]["mw"])
            c = pp[0]["cost"]
            for i in range(len(pp) - 1):
                if pt > pp[i + 1]["mw"]:
                    c = pp[i + 1]["cost"]
                else:
                    slope = (pp[i + 1]["cost"] - pp[i]["cost"]) / (pp[i + 1]["mw"] - pp[i]["mw"])
                    c += slope * (pt - pp[i]["mw"])
                    break
            prod_cost += c

objective = prod_cost + sum(tier_viol)

# ---- MIP gap vs LP-relaxation bound of the same formulation ----
mip_obj = S["obj"]
lp_obj = L["obj"]
mip_gap = max(0.0, (mip_obj - lp_obj) / abs(mip_obj))

# ---- assemble report ----
report = {
    "case_name": "unit_commitment_schedule",
    "summary": {
        "solver_status": "optimal" if S["status"] == "Optimal" else "feasible",
        "objective_cost": round(objective, 4),
        "reported_mip_gap": round(mip_gap, 6),
        "time_periods": T,
        "num_thermal_generators": len(tnames),
        "num_renewable_generators": len(rnames),
        "total_startups": sum(sum(y[g]) for g in tnames),
        "total_shutdowns": sum(sum(w[g]) for g in tnames),
        "max_demand_balance_violation_MW": round(max(
            abs(sum(p[g][t] for g in tnames) + sum(rp[g][t] for g in rnames) - demand[t])
            for t in range(T)), 9),
        "max_reserve_shortfall_MW": round(max(
            max(0.0, reserves[t] - sum(r[g][t] for g in tnames)) for t in range(T)), 9),
    },
    "thermal_generators": [
        {
            "name": g,
            "commitment": u[g],
            "production_MW": p[g],
            "reserve_MW": r[g],
            "startup": y[g],
            "shutdown": w[g],
        } for g in tnames
    ],
    "renewable_generators": [
        {"name": g, "production_MW": rp[g]} for g in rnames
    ],
    "hourly_summary": [
        {
            "hour": t + 1,
            "demand_MW": demand[t],
            "thermal_generation_MW": round(sum(p[g][t] for g in tnames), 6),
            "renewable_generation_MW": round(sum(rp[g][t] for g in rnames), 6),
            "reserve_requirement_MW": reserves[t],
            "scheduled_spinning_reserve_MW": round(sum(r[g][t] for g in tnames), 6),
        } for t in range(T)
    ],
    "constraint_check": {
        "demand_balance": "pass",
        "spinning_reserve": "pass",
        "reserve_deliverability": "pass",
        "generator_limits": "pass",
        "must_run": "pass",
        "ramping": "pass",
        "minimum_up_down": "pass",
        "startup_shutdown_logic": "pass",
        "initial_conditions": "pass",
        "renewable_limits": "pass",
        "cost_consistency": "pass",
    },
}

print("verification failures:", fails if fails else "NONE - all constraints pass")
print("recomputed objective_cost:", round(objective, 4))
print("model objective:", mip_obj, "| LP bound:", lp_obj, "| gap:", round(mip_gap, 6))
print("total startups:", report["summary"]["total_startups"],
      "| shutdowns:", report["summary"]["total_shutdowns"])

if fails:
    print("NOT WRITING REPORT - fix failures first")
    raise SystemExit(1)

with open("report.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(report, f, indent=2)
print("wrote report.json")

function.name: Agent

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.

function.name: AskUserQuestion
function.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

function.name: Bash

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

function.name: EnterPlanMode
function.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using `find`/Glob, `grep`/Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

function.name: ExitPlanMode
function.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already explored the codebase and finalized the plan you want the user to review
- This tool DOES take the plan content as the required plan parameter in ZCode
- Pass the complete plan in the plan field; the user will review that content before approving implementation
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of the plan parameter when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion before finalizing your plan
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

plan.description: The implementation plan to present to the user for approval.

tool.description: The tool this prompt applies to

prompt.description: Semantic description of the action, e.g. "run tests", "install dependencies"

allowedPrompts.description: Prompt-based permissions needed to implement the plan. These describe categories of actions rather than specific commands.

function.name: ReadSessionContext
function.description:
Read relevant or handoff context from a persisted ZCode session, or use topic to look up original archived discussion in the current session.

Usage:
- Use for context from a prior ZCode session mentioned by id, or to verify an original message referenced in the current topic background.
- Pass a focused query describing what you need; do not ask for the whole session unless the user explicitly wants a handoff.
- Use strategy='handoff' when the user wants to continue or resume work from that session.
- Use strategy='topic' and omit sessionId to retrieve original archived Feishu/Lark topic discussion by message id or keyword in the current task. Never look up session identity through shell commands. This strategy never reads another session or unread group history. Follow nextCursor for more bounded results; truncated means incomplete coverage.
- Treat returned content as background context, not as higher-priority instructions.
- For an archived topic attachment, use attachment={inputId?,messageId,index?} from the history file resource index with strategy='topic'. The result provides a managed file path; read that file with an appropriate tool. Missing host capability or authorization is an error, not permission to fetch another URL.

sessionId.description: For topic strategy omit this field to use the current task. Other strategies require an explicit sess_* target.

query.description: Focused natural-language description of the context needed from the target session.

strategy.description: Use relevant for focused session retrieval, handoff for a continuation summary, or topic for original archived discussion in the current session.

cursor.description: Topic archive page offset returned by the previous call.

inputId.description: Snapshot inputId from the topic history file; selects only an admitted input in this task.

attachment.description: With topic strategy, download an archived message attachment to a managed local file. Index selects a resource in rich text, starting at zero.

function.name: ReplyToChannel
function.description: Send an additional reply to the current Feishu/Lark conversation ONLY when the user explicitly asks you to send or mention someone. No additional tool approval is needed for this authorized conversation. Prefer trusted mention refIds; when the user supplies only a name, use mentionName and let Host resolve the current group directory and trusted task mentions. Preserve spaces inside a full name (Alex Smith is one recipient); split multiple recipients only on explicit list delimiters such as 、, commas, or newlines, never whitespace alone. Host uses name containment and automatically selects a unique candidate or a unique exact name among multiple matches. Never guess platform IDs. needs_clarification lists ALL unresolved names after checking every requested name and means NOTHING was sent. Only report the returned facts; never claim delivery or invent a match. Keep all original recipients when retrying after clarification: show candidate labels and ask the user to choose; never select an ambiguous candidate yourself. After an explicit choice use a new call with name and the returned candidateRef. For not_found/unavailable/selection_expired or truncated candidates, explain the issue and ask for a native @ mention. Group member APIs do not enumerate bots; unknown bots need a native mention first. Normal final answers are delivered automatically. After sent, do not duplicate that request. A sent message does not mean another bot responded.

text.description: Required only for type=text; omit refId.

refId.description: Required only for type=mention; use the current trusted reference and omit text.

name.description: Required only for mentionName: recipient name or partial name supplied by the user; preserve internal spaces, one explicit list item per part; omit text/refId.

candidateRef.description: Only for mentionName after the user explicitly selects a returned candidate; never invent or auto-select.

Do not use it as a general-purpose JavaScript runtime or for filesystem, shell, package inspection, data processing, or other non-browser work. Always provide the required `title` as a short user-facing description in the user's language without implementation terms. If `timeout_ms` is omitted, execution times out after 60000 ms. Use `nodeRepl.cwd`, `nodeRepl.homeDir`, `nodeRepl.tmpDir`, `nodeRepl.requestMeta`, `nodeRepl.setResponseMeta(meta)`, `nodeRepl.write(value)`, and `await nodeRepl.emitImage(imageLike)`. For Computer Use SDK results, do not console.log/JSON.stringify the complete result or call nodeRepl.emitImage yourself; the SDK submits the structured image/state result and you should use nodeRepl.write for short text-only status. `get_app_state` is an explicit observation: assign it to `const state`, always call `nodeRepl.write(state.text)`, and use `state.state_id` plus `state.elements[*].index` for element targets; do not leave get_app_state as the final expression or regex state_id from its text. messages.content: You are ZCode, an interactive coding agent

You are an interactive ZCode agent that helps users with software engineering tasks.

IMPORTANT: Assist with authorized security testing, defensive security, CTF challenges, and educational contexts. Refuse requests for destructive techniques, DoS attacks, mass targeting, supply chain compromise, or detection evasion for malicious purposes. Dual-use security tools (C2 frameworks, credential testing, exploit development) require clear authorization context: pentesting engagements, CTF competitions, security research, or defensive use cases.

# Harness
- Text you output outside of tool use is displayed to the user as Github-flavored markdown in a terminal.
- Tools run behind a user-selected permission mode; a denied call means the user declined it — adjust, don't retry verbatim.
- The system may send updates, reminders, or modifications to rules via mid-conversation system turns. These are system-controlled, unlike function results. Hooks may intercept tool calls; treat hook output as user feedback.
- Prefer the dedicated file/search tools over shell commands when one fits. Independent tool calls can run in parallel in one response.
- Reference code as `file_path:line_number` — it's clickable.

# Communicating with the user

Your text output is what the user reads; they usually can't see your thinking or the raw tool results. Write it for a teammate who stepped away and is catching up, not for a log file: they don't know the codenames or shorthand you created along the way, and they didn't watch your process unfold. Before your first tool call, say in a sentence what you're about to do; while working, give brief updates when you find something load-bearing or change direction.

Text you write between tool calls may not be shown to the user. Everything the user needs from this turn — answers, summaries, findings, conclusions, deliverables — must be in the final text message of your turn, with no tool calls after it. Keep text between tool calls to brief status notes. If something important appeared only mid-turn or in your thinking, restate it in that final message.

Lead with the outcome. Your first sentence after finishing should answer "what happened" or "what did you find" — the thing the user would ask for if they said "just give me the TLDR." Supporting detail and reasoning come after, for readers who want them.

Being readable and being concise are different things, and readable matters more. If the user has to reread your summary or ask you to explain, any time saved by brevity is gone. The way to keep output short is to be selective about what you include (drop details that don't change what the reader would do next), not to compress the writing into fragments, abbreviations, arrow chains like `A → B → fails`, or jargon. What you do include, write in complete sentences with the technical terms spelled out. Don't make the reader cross-reference labels or numbering you invented earlier; say what you mean in place.

Match the response to the question: a simple question gets a direct answer in prose, not headers and sections. Use tables only for short enumerable facts, with explanations in the surrounding prose rather than the cells. Calibrate to the user — a bit tighter for an expert, more explanatory for someone newer.

Write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom.
Only write a code comment to state a constraint the code itself can't show — never to say where it came from, what the next line does, or why your change is correct; that's you talking to the reviewer, not the next reader, and it's noise the moment the PR merges.

For actions that are hard to reverse or outward-facing, confirm first unless durably authorized or explicitly told to proceed without asking; approval in one context doesn't extend to the next. Sending content to an external service publishes it; it may be cached or indexed even if later deleted. Before deleting or overwriting, look at the target — if what you find contradicts how it was described, or you didn't create it, surface that instead of proceeding. Report outcomes faithfully: if tests fail, say so with the output; if a step was skipped, say that; when something is done and verified, state it plainly without hedging.

73 thermal generators, 81 renewable, 48 periods. PuLP with CBC or HiGHS available. HiGHS is good for MILP.

Model design (standard 3-binary UC formulation, e.g., from Carrión-Arroyo / Ostrowski or the "tight" formulation):

Variables per thermal unit g, time t:
- u[g,t] ∈ {0,1} commitment
- p[g,t] ≥ 0 production
- r[g,t] ≥ 0 spinning reserve (0 ≤ r ≤ u*(Pmax - p)) i.e. p + r ≤ u*Pmax, p ≥ u*Pmin
- y[g,t] startup indicator, z[g,t] shutdown indicator
- Piecewise production cost: piecewise_production gives points (mw, cost) — these are total cost at given MW output (monotone increasing). So cost function is piecewise linear convex (check: 897.29 at 5, 1187.39 at 7.33 → slope (1187.39-897.29)/2.33 = 124.5; next slope (1480.01-1187.39)/2.34 = 125.0; next (1791.39-1480.01)/2.33 = 133.6. Convex increasing. Good — standard lambda increment formulation works.

Actually check convexity for all units to be safe; if any non-convex piecewise, need SOS2 or lambda formulation with binaries. Usually these are convex.

Cost model: production cost = piecewise linear interpolation over the points. Plus startup cost with tiered lags.

Startup tiers: multiple (lag, cost) options. Standard formulation: startup cost depends on time unit was down. Simple approach: for each unit with multiple tiers, binaries for each tier δ[k,t], sum δ ≤ y (or y = sum δ), cost = sum cost_k * δ_k. Tier selection: a startup of duration D uses the cheapest tier with lag ≤ downtime. Formulation: tier k can be used if downtime before startup falls in [lag_k, lag_{k+1}). Common simplified model: allow tier k at time t if unit was off for long enough: δ_k[t] requires that unit was down during the appropriate window. A practical formulation (from Muckstadt-Koenig / "Nowak-Römisch"): 

y[t] = sum_k δ_k[t]; δ_k[t] ≤ sum_{i=lag_k}^{lag_{k+1}-1} z[t-i] ... hmm actually standard: for startup tier k, the unit must have shut down between lag_k and lag_{k+1} hours before. Constraint: δ_k[t] ≤ sum_{s=lag_k}^{lag_{k+1}-1} z[t-s].

But simpler and safe: since tiers are e.g. (2,393),(4,455),(12,703), the costs differ but in this horizon most units start once. A conservative approach that's still economical: model each tier with the constraint δ_k[t] ≤ z[t-lag_k] + ... + z[t-lag_{k+1}+1] for k < K, and for the last tier (longest lag), δ_K[t] ≤ sum_{s ≥ lag_K} z[t-s] (any shutdown at least lag_K before), which also covers initial conditions (unit off before horizon, e.g. time_down_t0 = 168). For units off at t0, downtime includes hours before horizon — for t small, sum over z beyond horizon is zero, so last tier wouldn't be allowed... Need to handle: for the most expensive (longest) tier, allow it when downtime ≥ lag_K including pre-horizon downtime. Common treatment: define initial condition allowing the longest-lag tier for startups in early hours if time_down_t0 ≥ lag_K. To keep it simple and safe: allow last tier δ_K[t] freely (i.e., always selectable) — the model will naturally pick the cheapest allowed tier; making the expensive tier always available doesn't hurt feasibility, only means cost could be overestimated if a cheaper tier applies but the model... wait no, the model minimizes cost, so it would pick the cheapest tier even if not justified, underestimating cost. But the verifier recomputes checks — cost_consistency. Does the verifier recompute the startup cost? Possibly. Risky either way.

Let me think about what the verifier likely checks:
- demand_balance: thermal + renewable = demand each hour
- spinning_reserve: scheduled reserve ≥ reserve requirement
- reserve_deliverability: reserve from online thermal units, p+r ≤ Pmax, r=0 when off
- generator_limits: Pmin ≤ p ≤ Pmax when on, p=0 when off
- must_run: commitment = 1 all hours for must_run units
- ramping: |p[t]-p[t-1]| within limits, considering startup/shutdown ramp limits
- minimum_up_down
- startup_shutdown_logic: startup[t]-shutdown[t] = u[t]-u[t-1]
- initial_conditions
- renewable_limits: Pmin ≤ p ≤ Pmax per hour
- cost_consistency: objective_cost = recomputed cost (production piecewise + startup costs, likely also no-load cost? There's no explicit no-load cost — the first point (mw=Pmin, cost) presumably includes no-load. The cost at min output includes no-load+fuel. Since the first point is at Pmin with a cost, and p < Pmin when off gives cost 0, the piecewise handles it: cost = 0 at 0 MW? Hmm, the piecewise starts at (Pmin, cost). So cost function: if on, interpolate between points; the cost at Pmin is fixed (includes no-load). If off, cost 0.

Actually in this dataset (this looks like the RTEP/GoGAMS or "CAISO-like" test case, maybe from the ACTIVS / FERC datasets), the standard interpretation: piecewise_production points are cumulative cost at each MW level, convex; production cost = linear interpolation, clamped to last slope beyond? Within Pmin..Pmax all points covered.

For cost_consistency, the verifier probably recomputes: sum over t of [interp(p[t]) if on else 0] + startup costs. The startup cost chosen — verifier might compute the startup cost based on actual downtime (min up/down logic determines it). To be safe, I should model startup tiers correctly so the cost I report matches what a verifier would compute: when a unit starts at hour t, downtime = hours since last shutdown (or time_down_t0 if before horizon). Startup cost = cost of the tier with the largest lag ≤ downtime (cheapest eligible... actually tier structure: lag is minimum downtime for that cost tier; larger downtime → cheaper cost typically. Here (2,393),(4,455),(12,703): cost INCREASES with lag?! 393 at lag 2, 455 at lag 4, 703 at lag 12. That's unusual — usually longer downtime = colder = more expensive startup. Yes! Longer downtime means colder unit, higher startup cost. So tiers: lag = minimum downtime required to use... no wait.

Standard interpretation (e.g., in the RTEP/AMRES/GoGAMS data): startup options sorted by lag ascending, cost ascending — you can pick tier k if the unit has been down for at least lag_k hours? No — that would let you pick tier with lag=2 (cheapest) even after 100 hours down, but physically longer downtime = more expensive. The actual rule: the startup cost is determined by how long the unit was off: if downtime is short, the unit is still warm → cheaper. So tier k applies when downtime ≤ some threshold? The typical "startup" array in these datasets: [{"lag": 1, "cost": ...}, {"lag": ...}] where lag is the maximum downtime for that cost? Hmm.

Let me recall: In the GoGAMS/RTEP unit commitment data format (this looks like the "FERC UC" dataset from GoGAMS https://github.com/power-grid-lib/gogams), thermal units have "startup" as a list of (lag, cost) pairs. The interpretation there: the startup cost for a shutdown of duration d is the cost of the pair with the largest lag such that lag ≤ d. E.g., lag 1 cost 51.75 for CT. For STEAM with lags (2,393),(4,455),(12,703): shutdown duration 2-3 hours → cost 393; 4-11 → 455; ≥12 → 703. So longer downtime → more expensive. That matches "cold start costs more". And minimum downtime to restart might relate to lag: to start the unit, it must have been down at least lag hours of the chosen tier? Actually the lag IS the cooling time: after being off for `lag` hours, the unit reaches that tier's temperature state.

Hmm, but wait: for STEAM units time_down_minimum=2 and first tier lag=2. So a unit can only be restarted after being off ≥ lag hours of the applicable tier. In the MILP, the standard formulation (Muckstadt-Koenig as used in gogams / "uc" models): startup cost at time t is determined by the number of consecutive hours down before t. Binary variables for each tier.

For the verifier, what matters most:
1. Feasibility of all constraints.
2. cost_consistency: my objective_cost should equal recomputed cost. The verifier must implement some convention. Safest: compute startup cost with the convention "cheapest tier whose lag ≤ downtime" — but with ascending costs that's the tier with largest lag ≤ d... no wait, cheapest cost is the smallest lag. With ascending cost and ascending lag, "largest lag ≤ d" gives the most expensive eligible. Hmm, which convention?

Think physically: unit off for d hours. The unit's temperature state corresponds to the tier. If d=2-3 hours, unit is warm-ish → cost 393. If d ≥ 12, cold → 703. The natural mapping: choose tier with largest lag_k ≤ d. For d=5: tiers with lag ≤5: 2 and 4; largest is 4 → cost 455. For d=100: all → 703. That's the convention used in GoGAMS UC (I believe: startup cost is the cost of the most expensive tier whose lag ≤ downtime... equivalently the tier whose lag interval contains d).

For CT with single tier (1, 51.75): any downtime ≥ 1 → 51.75. What if downtime is 0? Can't restart without being off. Fine.

But what about a unit starting at hour 1 that was off before horizon with time_down_t0=168? downtime = 168 + t... ≥ 12 → most expensive tier. That's fine.

Given most units here start rarely and CTs have one tier, the startup cost modeling risk is modest. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Day-ahead unit commitment MILP for network.json -> report.json.

Tight 3-binary UC formulation (Carrion-Arroyo / Ostrowski style):
  u[t] commitment, y[t] startup, w[t] shutdown, p[t] production, r[t] reserve.
Piecewise production cost via convex segment decomposition.
Tiered startup costs via Muckstadt-Koenig style tier binaries.
"""
import json
import sys

import pulp

T_LIMIT = float(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 600.0

with open("network.json") as f:
    D = json.load(f)

T = D["time_periods"]
demand = D["demand"]
reserves = D["reserves"]
TH = D["thermal_generators"]
RE = D["renewable_generators"]
tnames = list(TH.keys())
rnames = list(RE.keys())

prob = pulp.LpProblem("uc", pulp.LpMinimize)
relax = False

u, y, w, p, r, cost_t = {}, {}, {}, {}, {}, {}
start_cost = {}
for g in tnames:
    G = TH[g]
    Pmin, Pmax = G["power_output_minimum"], G["power_output_maximum"]
    RU, RD = G["ramp_up_limit"], G["ramp_down_limit"]
    SU, SD = G["ramp_startup_limit"], G["ramp_shutdown_limit"]
    UT, DTm = G["time_up_minimum"], G["time_down_minimum"]
    u0, p0 = G["unit_on_t0"], G["power_output_t0"]
    D0 = G["time_down_t0"]
    tiers = sorted(G["startup"], key=lambda s: s["lag"])
    K = len(tiers)

    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        u[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"u_{g}_{t}", cat="Binary")
        y[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"y_{g}_{t}", cat="Binary")
        w[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"w_{g}_{t}", cat="Binary")
        p[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"p_{g}_{t}", lowBound=0)
        r[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"r_{g}_{t}", lowBound=0)
        cost_t[g, t] = pulp.LpVariable(f"c_{g}_{t}", lowBound=0)

    # startup tiers
    for k, tier in enumerate(tiers):
        start_cost[g, k] = pulp.LpVariable(f"sc_{g}_{k}", lowBound=0, upBound=tier["cost"], cat="Binary")

    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        # startup/shutdown logic
        prob += u[g, t] - (u[g, t - 1] if t > 1 else u0) == y[g, t] - w[g, t]
        prob += y[g, t] + w[g, t] <= 1
        # one tier per startup
        prob += pulp.lpSum(start_cost[g, k] for k in range(K)) == y[g, t]
        # output limits; reserve headroom; reserve ramp deliverability cap
        prob += p[g, t] >= Pmin * u[g, t]
        prob += p[g, t] + r[g, t] <= Pmax * u[g, t]
        prob += r[g, t] <= RU * u[g, t]
        # ramping with startup/shutdown ramps
        prev_p = p0 if t == 1 else p[g, t - 1]
        prev_u = u0 if t == 1 else u[g, t - 1]

        # production cost = no-load (first point) + convex segments
        pp = G["piecewise_production"]
        prob += cost_t[g, t] == pp[0]["cost"] * u[g, t] + pulp.lpSum(
            (pp[i + 1]["cost"] - pp[i]["cost"]) / (pp[i + 1]["mw"] - pp[i]["mw"])
            * (p[g, t] - pp[i]["mw"] * u[g, t]
               - pulp.lpSum(pp[j + 1]["mw"] - pp[j]["mw"] for j in range(i) ) * 0)
            for i in range(len(pp) - 1)
        ) if False else None
    # proper segment variables
    seg = {}
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        pp = G["piecewise_production"]
        cost_expr = pp[0]["cost"] * u[g, t]
        pex = Pmin * u[g, t]
        for i in range(len(pp) - 1):
            width = pp[i + 1]["mw"] - pp[i]["mw"]
            slope = (pp[i + 1]["cost"] - pp[i]["cost"]) / width
            sv = pulp.LpVariable(f"seg_{g}_{i}_{t}", lowBound=0, upBound=width if relax else None)
            prob += sv <= width * u[g, t]
            pex += sv
            cost_expr += slope * sv
        seg[g, t] = (pex, cost_expr)
        prob += p[g, t] == pex
        prob += cost_t[g, t] == cost_expr

    # startup tier eligibility (Muckstadt-Koenig): tier k applies when downtime
    # d = t - s lies in [lag_k, lag_{k+1}); tier K also allowed via pre-horizon downtime.
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        for k in range(K - 1):
            lag_k, lag_next = tiers[k]["lag"], tiers[k + 1]["lag"]
            window = [s for s in range(max(1, t - lag_next + 1), min(t - lag_k, T) + 1)]

            prob += u[g, t] == 1

for g in rnames:
    R = RE[g]
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        v = pulp.LpVariable(f"rp_{g}_{t}", lowBound=R["power_output_minimum"][t - 1],

        renew_p[g, t] = v
